source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19:265-288
finding: Founding claim: take the socio-technical system (the cockpit), not the person, as the unit of analysis. Ask the usual cognitive questions (how are representations stored, transformed, propagated) of that larger unit. Many representations can be watched directly because they sit outside heads.
numbers: Basis: more than 100 observer flights over 6 years in commercial cockpits (old and new tech, domestic and trans-oceanic). Worked case: MD-80 descent, ILS approach, landing.
quote: a socio-technical system rather than an individual mind as its primary unit of analysis
limits: The account is stylised, not a raw observation log; the author says he chose not to present extended real examples. No quantitative test of the theory.
agent_relevance: Our agent is one model plus tools. The cockpit view says: count notes, files and checks as part of the thinking system, and design them as memory, not as logs.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19:265-288
finding: The cockpit remembers approach speeds through a chain of media. A gross-weight readout selects a speed card; the PNF says the speeds aloud; both pilots set speed bugs on two airspeed indicators; later the needle-versus-bug relation tells when to extend flaps. Each medium has different durability: card booklet permanent, speech ephemeral, bugs durable for this approach.
numbers: Speed card for 122,000 lb: min-man speeds 227 (0/RET), 177 (0/EXT), 155 (11), 152 (15), 142 (28), 137 (40); Vref 132 (28/EXT) and 128 (40/EXT). Bugs set about 25-30 min before landing at light workload, used 10-15 min later. One card per about 2,000 lb band. PNF calls out deviations over 5 knots at 500 ft AFL.
limits: Numbers describe one aircraft type and one airline procedure.
agent_relevance: Pattern to copy: compute once in a low-load phase, save the result in a durable external object, read it back by cheap perceptual match later. A scratch file or computed table does this for an agent.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19:265-288
finding: Speed bugs do not improve pilot memory. They replace a memory task (remember speeds, read the dial, compare numbers) with a cheaper perceptual one (is the needle near the bug). The memory function becomes a property of the larger system.
quote: Individual pilot memory has not been enhanced; rather, the memory function has now become a property of a larger system
limits: Interpretive argument from observation and task analysis. No experiment compares crews with and without bugs.
agent_relevance: Do not judge a scaffold by whether the model remembers more. Judge whether the task became an easier operation. Supports our rule that code, not the model, holds counts and state.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19:265-288
finding: Cognitive labour is distributed three ways: across people (PF flies, PNF reads airspeed and speaks it, turning visual into auditory information), across time (compute in low workload, use later), and across media. Procedure also gives redundancy: two bug sets, spoken cross-checks, checklist challenge/response.
numbers: Author reports crews always computed and set approach speeds in all his observations.
quote: never have I seen a crew fail to compute and set the approach speeds
limits: The no-failure claim is the author's observation, not a counted rate. The text says crews sometimes do miss it and make headlines.
agent_relevance: Redundancy by independent media is the point. Two copies from one model are not independent (our G4); a code check or a different representation is.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19:265-288
finding: Opportunistic use of structure: pilots use the width of the salmon bug as a yardstick on the dial. Designers never specified it as a tool; it exists so the bug never hides more than one 10-knot tick.
numbers: Salmon bug base fits between large ticks at 10-knot intervals (Boeing 757/767 airspeed indicator, as reported by the engineer).
quote: Using the width of the salmon bug as a yardstick in local speed space is a wonderful example
limits: Single anecdote from one engineer interview.
agent_relevance: Agents also use unintended affordances (tool output formats, file names as state). A method for studying our agent: log what it does with tools beyond their purpose.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for human-computer interaction research. ACM TOCHI 7(2) (author revision, April 2000)
finding: States two principles. (1) The unit of analysis is set by functional relations among elements, not by being inside one skull. (2) Cognitive processes include more than symbol manipulation inside actors: they involve equipment and environment. Three kinds of distribution: across group members, between internal and external structure, and through time.
limits: Programme paper, not an empirical study.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist for describing any agent system: who or what holds each piece of state, and how it moves.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for human-computer interaction research. ACM TOCHI 7(2) (author revision, April 2000)
finding: Defines cognitive ethnography as event-centred, not a single technique. It mixes interviews, surveys, participant observation, video and audio recording. It differs from 1960s-70s cognitive anthropology, which studied what people know and mostly ignored action. Real domain commitment and expertise are required; observation supplies phenomena the theory must explain.
quote: Cognitive ethnography is not any single data collection or analysis technique.
limits: Only a stance; no coding manual, inter-rater procedure or sampling rule.
agent_relevance: No ready LLM analogue yet. Closest: reading full agent transcripts of what it does with tools and files, not only final answers.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for human-computer interaction research. ACM TOCHI 7(2) (author revision, April 2000)
finding: Proposed research loop: observation, theory, design of work materials, new observation; experiments are 'ethnographically natural' tests of changes in naturally varying parameters. Example: ethnography of airspeed indicators found pilots rarely read speed as a number, so a digital airspeed tape was designed and eye-movement tests were planned.
limits: Plans, not test results, for the airspeed tape.
agent_relevance: Same loop fits our work: watch agent runs, form a hypothesis about a failure, change the scaffold, watch again. Keep the observation step real, with logs.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for human-computer interaction research. ACM TOCHI 7(2) (author revision, April 2000)
finding: Ship-navigation ethnography (1980s, US Navy): outcomes that mattered were not determined by any single navigator but by interactions among several. It also compared Western and Micronesian navigation traditions to show one computational level of description can cover very different representational systems.
limits: Summarised from the author's own earlier work, not new data.
agent_relevance: Different representations compute the same thing with different easy and hard inferences. Our schema's representation choice shapes what the model finds easy.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for human-computer interaction research. ACM TOCHI 7(2) (author revision, April 2000)
finding: Design argument: the newest cockpit (Boeing 737-700) reproduces the old electro-mechanical instrument on a digital display; the authors take this as sign of design not grounded in cognitive ethnography. People shift between attending to the representation and the thing represented.
limits: Argument by example; no safety or error measure in the text read.
agent_relevance: Warning against copying a human tool into an agent without knowing what work it did.

source: Hutchins (1995) Cognition in the Wild, MIT Press (book not read; author's site page read)
finding: Book-length ethnography of navigation on US Navy ships. The author's page says he went to sea on a series of ships studying bridge navigation. Main claim: a navigation team is a cognitive system whose computation spreads over people, charts, instruments and talk. The page also lists sibling papers (1990, 1991, 1993; Seifert & Hutchins 1992 Error as opportunity).
numbers: Team size, fix cycle length and error counts are in the book; not verified here.
limits: Book not opened. Treat details as pointers, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Still the founding text; read it before quoting any number.

source: Hutchins project pages: Robust navigation; Micronesian navigation
finding: Later work digitised the ship video and reanalysed how the system adapts to perturbations; hypothesis that robustness comes partly from how navigators use their bodies. Micronesian navigators imagine the canoe still while islands move, which reduces the complexity of relating canoe, islands and star frame.
limits: Project pages only, no results. The author says he could not sail with these navigators, so his account of their technique is not certain.
agent_relevance: Frame choice (what moves, what stays fixed) changes difficulty. Relevant to a reframe operator.

source: Hutchins & Hinton (1984) Why the islands move. Perception 13:629-632; Hutchins (1983) Understanding Micronesian navigation
finding: The etak scheme: the canoe is held fixed under the stars and a reference island moves from one star bearing to the next. Western researchers called it illogical; Hutchins argues it is a different frame with different easy and hard inferences. Only the citation and the 2005 retelling were read.
limits: Papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Cognitive ethnography corrected a verdict of irrationality. Caution when grading odd-looking model reasoning.

source: Hutchins (2005) Material anchors for conceptual blends. Journal of Pragmatics
finding: Thinking needs stable representations of constraints. Stability comes from cultural models shared among people, or from tying concepts to material structure. A material anchor is an input space that projects material structure into a conceptual blend: queues, method of loci, calendars, star-bearing navigation, number lines. Anchors vary in presence needed, complexity, and designed versus opportunistic use.
numbers: Cites Wason four-card task; for a related reasoning item about 15% of subjects chose the correct conclusion (figure quoted from earlier work).
quote: Projecting material structure into a blended space can stabilize the conceptual blend.
limits: Conceptual framework with cases, no measured test. The 15% figure is from prior work.
agent_relevance: Direct link to our design: reasoning is only as stable as its anchors. A written constraint list, a test file or a table is an anchor. Unanchored constraints may drift over long runs.

source: Hutchins (2013) The cultural ecosystem of human cognition. Philosophical Psychology
finding: Moves from single extended-mind assemblies to the cultural-cognitive ecosystem. A family of practices project an imagined trajector onto a spatial array (queues, constellations, method of loci, reading, number line, flight-deck chart reading). Conjecture: cultural practices reduce entropy (raise predictability) at all scales, which suits a predicting brain.
limits: Conjectures and intuition pumps. The entropy claim is not tested here (cites Hutchins 2012).
agent_relevance: Suggests a scaffold should make the model's input stream predictable: fixed formats, stable slots, repeated structure.

source: Hutchins (2013) The cultural ecosystem of human cognition (flight-deck data section)
finding: Instrumented digital cognitive ethnography: a qualified crew flew a scenario in a high-fidelity Boeing 787 simulator. The lab recorded multiple HD video streams, digital audio, digital pen data, wearable eye tracking on both pilots, and simulator data. Vignette: the first officer says 'after Helens, then we're gonna go to Battle Ground' while fixating chart waypoints, while the captain looks at the empty waypoint slot on the computer.
numbers: One crew, a few seconds of activity; fixations about 0.5 s, 0.5 s and almost 1 s.
limits: One crew, one vignette. Illustrates the method; no rate or effect size.
agent_relevance: Template for studying an agent: many synchronised streams (prompt, tool calls, files, outputs) read together, then micro-analysis of a short episode.

source: Alac & Hutchins (2004) I see what you are saying: action as cognition in fMRI brain mapping practice. Journal of Cognition and Culture 4(3)
finding: Cognitive ethnography at micro scale on video. Scientists make fMRI images meaningful through gesture, speech and material structure together. In 'learning to see retinotopy' the expert traces V1 borders on a paper chart, then repeats the trace on the brain image, performing the mapping as visible action. The unit of analysis is the whole multimodal complex.
numbers: Three labs, 15 participants, nine months of ethnography; the analysed episode chosen from eight hours of video.
quote: The method of cognitive ethnography combines traditional long-term participant observation with the micro-analysis of specific occurrences
limits: Episode chosen because it made practice explicit; no counts, no coder agreement, one episode analysed in depth. Warrant comes from the long ethnography.
agent_relevance: Video coding in this field is interpretation of single episodes, not coded frequencies. An LLM coder would need the long-term context as input.

source: Bender, Hutchins & Medin (2010) Anthropology in cognitive science. Topics in Cognitive Science 2:374-385
finding: History: cognitive anthropology (1950s-70s) put culture in the head. D'Andrade (1981) split labour: psychology studies how people think, anthropology what they think. That left the material and social world as something people think about, not with. The field drifted from cognitive science as sociocultural anthropology turned humanist; distributed cognition is part of the attempted return.
limits: History by interested authors, no data.
agent_relevance: Context only: why the method is rare in cognitive science and why evidence is mostly case studies.

source: Hutchins & Hazlehurst (1991) Learning in the cultural process; (1995) How to invent a lexicon; Hazlehurst & Hutchins (1998) Emergence of propositions
finding: Computational models: communities of connectionist networks that learn while building external structures that mediate each other's behaviour. From the abstracts: over generations such a system yields agents with abilities no single agent reaches in a lifetime; a lexicon arises from convergence of classification schemes under pressure for consensus; propositional structure emerges from coordinating joint attention in time.
numbers: No numbers in the abstracts as read.
limits: Only abstracts on the project page were read. Toy worlds; the stated aim is to clarify theory, not replicate a real culture.
agent_relevance: Early formal model of cultural process. Ancestor of multi-agent LLM studies of emergent shared conventions.

source: Fouse, Weibel, Hutchins & Hollan (2011) ChronoViz; Weibel et al. (2012) eye-tracking tools (as cited in Hutchins 2013)
finding: The Hutchins lab built digital tools for cognitive ethnography: navigation of time-coded multi-stream data (CHI 2011) and eye-tracking integration (ETRA 2012). The 2013 article cites them but reports no measured performance.
limits: Read only the citation and description, not the CHI or ETRA papers.
agent_relevance: Software for synchronised multi-stream coding exists; an LLM assistant could plug into the same data model. No tested result in what I read.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science 18:513-549 (not opened)
finding: Recalled, not verified: expert Tetris players rotate pieces on screen to ease computation, even when mental rotation could give the same information. They call these epistemic actions. Part of the theory base the HCI paper builds on; see sibling subfield 07_epistemic_actions.
limits: Not opened; check sibling note before quoting numbers.
agent_relevance: Agents do epistemic actions when they run code to look at a value instead of guessing. Our schema already favours this.

source: Jordan & Henderson (1995) Interaction analysis: foundations and practice. J. Learning Sciences 4(1) (not opened)
finding: Recalled, not verified: group video analysis from Xerox PARC and IRL. Several analysts watch tape together with a list of foci (use of space, turn-taking, artifacts, disruptions); claims are checked by group viewing, not a coder-agreement statistic.
limits: Not opened; no numbers.
agent_relevance: If an LLM codes video or transcripts, the human benchmark is a group process, not one labeller. Agreement with one human is a weak test.

source: Hutchins & Klausen (1996) Distributed cognition in an airline cockpit. In Engestrom & Middleton (eds) Cognition and communication at work, pp 15-34 (not opened)
finding: Listed on the author's site as a core aviation paper. Only the citation was read; content not verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Fetch before use; likely the best worked example of coding real crew talk.

source: Hutchins project pages: Distributed cognition in aviation; A320 expertise
finding: Aviation lines: the Integrated Mode Management Interface (1994) was tested head-to-head against the 747-400 mode control panel in a NASA Ames simulator; later work on what pilots learn about autoflight on the line, with a redesign of an Airbus A320 managed-descent training module. Stated design principle: important conceptual distinctions should be salient perceptual distinctions.
numbers: IMMI comparison results are not on the page. Vertical profile display later nominated for an Aviation Week Laurel (2005).
limits: Summary web pages only.
agent_relevance: Shows the method fed real design cycles, but no effect sizes in what I read.

source: An (2025) Cognitive Workspace: active memory management for LLMs. arXiv 2508.13171
finding: LLM paper that cites Hutchins' distributed cognition, Clark's extended mind and Baddeley's working memory, and builds actively managed external memory buffers. Claims 54-60% memory reuse versus 0% for RAG and 17-18% net efficiency gain despite 3.3x more operations.
numbers: Corpus: 8 AI-domain documents; GPT-3.5-turbo. 4-round dialogue: reuse 54.52%, 99 vs 30 operations. 10-round: 57.1%, net 17.3%, t(18)=69.60. Multi-hop: 58.8%, net 17.9%, d=189.97. Conflict resolution: 59.8%, net 17.8%, d=195.66. Reported Cohen d 23 to 196.
quote: Net efficiency = reuse rate / (1 + extra operation ratio).
limits: Reuse rate is the paper's own metric and RAG scores 0 by construction. Tiny corpus, old model, no answer-quality score, implausible effect sizes. The link to Hutchins is rhetorical; no ethnography done. Treat as weak.
agent_relevance: Warning example: an active-memory result that never measures task accuracy. If we cite distributed cognition for our scaffold we must measure correctness, not reuse.

source: Osler (forthcoming; arXiv 2512.03682) Knowing oneself through and with AI: from self-tracking to chatbots
finding: Philosophical chapter using distributed cognition to analyse self-tracking apps, digital autobiographical memory and narrative co-construction with LLMs. Warns of narrative deference and narratives detached from reality.
limits: Conceptual; no data from LLM use.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrails against deferring to a stated answer (G5 conformity). No measured effect.

source: Search listing (arXiv, Nov 2026): Thinking with Many Minds (2501.02348); Theater of Mind (2604.08206)
finding: Seen only as one-line search-result summaries: multi-perspective LLM debate and a global-workspace multi-agent design. Neither summary names Hutchins, cognitive ethnography or video coding; I could not confirm they test this subfield.
limits: Not opened; do not count as evidence here.
agent_relevance: Probably belong to collective-intelligence and global-workspace families.

source: Search note: LLM use for coding video or field notes in cognitive ethnography
finding: Two arXiv search-page queries (distributed cognition + language model; cognitive ethnography) found no LLM study that tests cognitive ethnography on agents. The one 'cognitive ethnography' hit from a page summary turned out, when I opened the PDF, to be a survey experiment on populist messages (195 participants), so I dropped it. Gap in this pass; Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv APIs were rate-limited.
limits: Absence from a thin search, not proof of absence. Another angle's file (evidence_c.jsonl) may hold LLM video-analysis studies.
agent_relevance: Report as an open gap.
